l0_0.name: Tree — UI is basically a tree
l0_0.desc: Every HTML page is a nested structure, and a nested object can create exactly that shape.
l0_0.what:
A tree means: something inside something else, and more inside that. That's it.

Look at your HTML — a <div> containing a <h1> and a <ul>, and the <ul> containing three <li>. This is a tree. The topmost element is the root, the inner ones are children, and the ones with nothing inside are leaf.

Analogy: a cupboard with 3 drawers, each drawer with 2 boxes, each box with items. cupboard = root, drawer = children, items = leaf.

Now we can create the same shape with a JS object. And this is the foundation of the entire library — because we will create objects instead of writing HTML, and later generate real HTML from those objects.
l0_0.why:
If UI is an object, then comparing, copying, modifying UI becomes purely data work, not DOM work. Manipulating data is 100 times cheaper than manipulating the DOM. React’s entire speed comes from this idea.

How to do it:

A node should have two things: what it is (type), and what is inside it (children). Any extra info — class, id, onClick — put it in props.

Keep every node’s shape the same. Same shape means a single function can handle everything. This is a design decision, not a constraint — and it will cut your work in half.
gotchas: Don’t just log and assume you understand. Draw the tree on paper — who is whose parent. It will take 5 minutes and will help throughout the library.
Always keep children as an array, even if there is only one child. Switching between array and single object would require extra if statements in every function.

l0_1.name: Recursion — a function that calls itself
l0_1.desc: The natural way to work with trees. Forget the base case and the stack will explode.
l0_1.what:
Recursion means a function that calls itself inside its own body.

It is used when the problem can be broken into "smaller versions of the same problem". A tree is exactly that: process the whole tree = process the root + the same work for each child.

Analogy: you need to empty a cupboard. You say "empty every drawer". Emptying a drawer means "empty every box". Emptying a box means "remove the items". One instruction repeated at every level.

There are two parts: base case (when to stop) and recursive case (how to reduce). Forgetting the base case means the function never stops and the browser will throw Maximum call stack size exceeded.
l0_1.why:
Our render() function will be recursive — the whole thing in Stage A. Later, the biggest lesson in Stage C will be that you cannot stop recursion. Therefore, understanding recursion from the inside is essential, not just "it works".

How to do it:

Think like this: assume the function already works. Just write what to do "for one node" and "call yourself for the children". Don’t think about the whole tree — think about a single node.

And yes — the browser stores each recursive call in a call stack. The deeper the tree, the taller the stack.
gotchas: Write the base case first, and only then the recursive call. Writing them in reverse can sometimes accidentally create an infinite loop.

Placing await/return in the wrong place inside a for loop causes only the first child to be processed. The result is incomplete but no error is thrown — therefore always verify the output by counting.
A very deep tree (10,000 levels) will crash with plain recursion. This is the real reason for Stage C.
l0_1.visualCap: Call stack: each inner call climbs on top. No call finishes until the deepest call returns — therefore pausing recursion in the middle is impossible.

l0_2.name: Closure — a function’s private box
l0_2.desc: A function remembers variables from its outer scope. useState is built on exactly this.
l0_2.what:
When you create a function inside another function, the inner function remembers the outer function’s variables — even after the outer function has finished executing. This is called a closure.

Analogy: you entered a room, wrote a number on a slip, and closed the room. Now you have a small window through which you can read and modify that slip. No one else can see the slip. That window = closure.

Definition: A closure is a function bundled together with references to the variables from the scope in which it was created.
l0_2.why:
The whole magic of useState is this. The component function runs repeatedly, but the state remains "remembered" outside, and setState is a small function that has a window to that memory. Understanding closures makes hooks click in 10 minutes.

How to do it:

The most common pattern: a "factory" function that creates some variables and returns small functions that can touch them. The outside only receives those small functions — not the variable directly.

This is encapsulation — hiding data and exposing only controlled paths. The oldest and most useful approach in library design.
gotchas: If you use var inside a loop, all closures will capture the same variable. Use let — each iteration gets its own variable.
A closure does not "freeze" the old value; it points to the variable. If the variable changes, the closure sees the new value. This is the root of stale-state bugs.

l0_3.name: The 7 DOM functions we will use repeatedly
l0_3.desc: The entire library builds the DOM using only these calls. No magic.
l0_3.what:
Browser provides some simple functions that let you create and modify page elements. React uses these — just thoughtfully and very sparingly.

Our entire library will operate with only these 7:

  • document.createElement("div") — create a new element
  • document.createTextNode("hi") — node with only text
  • parent.appendChild(child) — insert inside
  • parent.removeChild(child) — remove
  • parent.replaceChild(naya, purana) — replace
  • el.addEventListener / removeEventListener — click etc.
  • el.setAttribute / removeAttribute — class, id etc.
l0_3.why:
Knowing that "the DOM only has these tools" gives you confidence. When you read React’s source, you will see only these 7 calls. There is no hidden API.

How to do it:

An important point: attributes and properties are different. setAttribute("value", "hi") writes to the HTML; el.value = "hi" changes the actual live value. For inputs you need the property, otherwise the user’s typed text will be reset.

Similarly, class exists in HTML but the JS property name is className — because class is a reserved word in JS. React adopted that name, so we will use it as well.
gotchas: Don’t use setAttribute("value", x) for inputs. Use el.value = x, otherwise whatever the user is typing will disappear.
removeEventListener works only when you pass exactly the same function reference that was given to addEventListener. Creating a new arrow function will cause remove to silently fail.
Creating DOM with innerHTML seems fast but it rebuilds everything each time — focus, scroll, event listeners all disappear. This entire project exists to solve that problem.

l0_4.name: Reference vs copy — and immutability
l0_4.desc: Changing an object versus creating a new object — they are worlds apart.
l0_4.what:
In JS an object is a reference — meaning the variable holds not the object itself, but its "address". Two variables can point to the same object.

Mutation = modify the same object (obj.x = 5). Immutability = leave the old one, create a new object ({...obj, x: 5}).

Analogy: mutation means overwriting on the same page of a book. Immutability means writing on a new page while keeping the old page unchanged. The old page will remain so you can compare what changed.
l0_4.why:
Our reconciler will compare the old tree and the new tree. If we mutate the old tree, there is nothing left to compare — both will look the same and no update will occur. This is the trickiest bug in Stage B and it happens silently, without an error.

How to do it:

Remember two cheap checks:

Object.is / === compare two references, not the inner content. That is why creating a new object lets React immediately know that "something changed".

Shallow compare means looking only one level deep. The useEffect deps array performs a shallow compare — so if you put a new object in the deps on every render, the effect will run each time.
gotchas: Array methods come in two types: push/splice/sort modify the existing array, map/filter/concat return a new one. Always use the latter for UI.
If you copy a nested object with {...obj}, only the top level is copied — inner objects are still shared.

l1_0.name: Imperative vs Declarative
l1_0.desc: Old approach: specify every step. New approach: specify the destination.
l1_0.what:
Imperative means you tell the browser every step: "find this div, change its text, remove this button's class, add this li."

Declarative means you only specify how the screen should look right now. How to get there is the library's responsibility.

Analogy: imperative = telling a taxi driver every turn ("turn left here, now right, now straight"). Declarative = just giving the address. Giving the address is better because when traffic changes you don't have to do anything.
l1_0.why:
Bugs appear in imperative code because you have to handle every possible transition. With 3 states there are 6 transitions. With 5 states there are 20. In declarative code you only write 5 "how the screen should look" specifications — the library derives the transitions. The place for bugs disappears.

How to do it:

To make it declarative, the library must know both the current screen and the desired screen so it can compute the difference. This is called reconciliation — and it is the heart of the whole project.

In other words, the cost of declarative UI is that the library has to remember the previous UI. Remember this trade-off — memory is spent to reduce code complexity.
gotchas: Declarative does not mean "slow". It is slow only when the library rebuilds everything on each update — fixing that is the job of Stage B.
Imperative bugs can still creep into declarative code if you reach into the DOM with document.querySelector and manipulate it. There should be a single owner of the DOM.

l1_1.name: UI = f(state)
l1_1.desc: A formula that is the contract of the entire library.
l1_1.what:
One line: what is displayed on the screen is only a function of the data.

That means if you give me your state object, I can tell exactly how the screen will look. The screen should not have any hidden memory.

Definition: UI = f(state) means the rendered output is a pure function of application state — same state in, same UI out, no hidden memory in the DOM.
l1_1.why:
This contract makes everything possible. Because of it, time-travel debugging, server rendering, hot reload, testing — all become possible. And because of it you can change state without fear, as the library will correctly re-render the screen.

How to do it:

This simply means our library’s public API has only two things: a way to describe the UI (createElement) and a way to change state (setState). Everything else is internal.

And there is a hidden rule: f must be pure — same state yields same output, and no side effects in between (fetch, timer, DOM manipulation). Side effects need a separate place — that’s why useEffect exists.
gotchas: Don’t place fetch, setTimeout or document.title = … inside a component. That makes the function impure and it will run twice if the render happens twice.
Don’t treat the DOM as state. "What is typed in an input" should be in state, not read from the DOM.

l1_2.name: Our library’s 4 layers
l1_2.desc: The blueprint of the whole project — look at it now, then each phase will find its place.
l1_2.what:
People think of React as a single thing, but it actually consists of four separate layers, one on top of another. We will build the same four, in that order.

1. Element layer — createElement. Describes the UI as a plain object. It has no knowledge of the DOM.
2. Renderer layer — render. Turns the object tree into the real DOM. Browser-specific.
3. Reconciler layer — compares old vs new and derives the minimal changes. This is the most brainy part.
4. Scheduler layer — breaks work into small chunks so the browser doesn’t get blocked.
l1_2.why:
Keeping them separate is not just for cleanliness — that’s why React Native exists. Layers 1, 3 and 4 stay the same; only layer 2 changes (DOM replaced by native views). This is the biggest lesson of the architecture: separate what can change.

How to do it:

We will deliberately build in three stages, so you can feel the need for each next layer yourself:

Stage A = layers 1 + 2 (createElement + render). It works, but everything is rebuilt on each update.
Stage B = add layer 3 (reconciler + hooks). Now only the necessary DOM changes, and state is available.
Stage C = add layer 4 (Fiber + scheduler). Even large trees won’t block the page.

At the end of each stage there is a phase called "wall" — there we will deliberately break things to show where the current stage fails. That will be your answer to "why the requirement arose".
gotchas: Don’t put everything in one file. Keep each layer in a separate file, even if the file is small — the real lesson is knowing which layer knows what.
The app folder should not import internal parts of the library. If you need to, your public API is incomplete.

l2_0.name: Element object — only three things
l2_0.desc: type, props, children. That's it. And children live inside props.
l2_0.what:
Virtual DOM element is a plain object that says "this thing should be here". It is not the actual DOM node — it is just a note.

Definition: A virtual DOM element is a lightweight plain-object description of a piece of UI. It is a description, not a thing.

Analogy: architect's blueprint vs actual house. Making a blueprint costs 10 rupees, building a house costs 1,000,000. So you can make 20 blueprints and discard them — no problem. Don't build the house 20 times. React does exactly this: blueprint is cheap, house is expensive.

Shape will be: { type, props } where props.children is an array. Keeping children inside props is a deliberate decision — it gives the component children as a regular prop.
l2_0.why:
This object is the thing we will compare in Stage B and process in chunks in Stage C. Keeping its shape simple and uniform later saves thousands of lines of complexity.

How to do it:

createElement(type, props, ...children). With the rest parameter (...children) you can provide as many children as you want. props can be null — in that case create an empty object.

And a small but important decision: if a child is a string or number, also turn it into an element whose type is "TEXT_ELEMENT". This makes every child's shape identical.

typeof null === "object" (a legacy JavaScript quirk). Therefore you need a separate check that child !== null.
props becomes null when you write createElement("h1", null, ...). {...null} yields an empty object — this works, but write it consciously.

l2_1.name: TEXT_ELEMENT — turning text into an element
l2_1.desc: A small decision that saves four "if" statements later.
l2_1.what:
The simplest approach is: leave a string in children as-as, and during render check "if it is a string, create a text node".

We won't do that. We will also turn a string into an element object with type "TEXT_ELEMENT". Now render, reconcile, commit — all receive the same shape.
l2_1.why:
This is called a uniform representation, and it is the biggest practical lesson in library design: by creating an extra object you avoid special-case branches in 10 places. Every special case is a spot where a bug can hide. React's actual code handles text slightly differently (for performance), but we will choose simplicity — and document this trade-off in decisions.md.

How to do it:

The name nodeValue is chosen deliberately — it is also the name of the DOM text node’s property. This lets us copy props directly in render without any mapping.

Also always keep children: [], even if text never has children. Because node.props.children.map(...) will run everywhere without a check.
gotchas: Do not turn false, null, or undefined into TEXT_ELEMENT — React does not render them. {cond && <div/>} should not print "false" on the screen. Filter them out.
Do not filter out 0! In {count && <div/>} when count is 0, React prints "0". When doing falsy checks, preserve 0 and "".

l2_2.desc: Purity and separation — layer 1 should not even know about the browser.
l2_2.what:
createElement is a pure function: given the same input it returns the same output, and it changes nothing in the world. No DOM, no global variables.

It has three major benefits, and all are used in the real world:

1. Testing becomes trivial — no browser needed, just compare objects.
2. It can run on the server — server-side rendering is possible because of this. There is no DOM on the server.

The small reward for maintaining purity is that your library can run anywhere.

l3_1.name: Applying props — the real complexity is here
l3_1.desc: Attribute, property, event, style, children — five different kinds of props.
l3_1.what:
"Apply props" sounds like one line, but props come in five types and each requires different handling:

1. children — this is not a prop, skip it.
2. Events (onClick) — addEventListener("click", fn).
3. style object — {color:"red"} should become dom.style.color = "red".
4. Live properties (value, checked) — dom.value = x, not setAttribute.
5. Everything else (className, id) — property assignment.
l3_1.why:
In React’s source there is a whole file for this (DOMPropertyOperations), and the reason is that the mapping between HTML/DOM is not clear. Understanding that “a large part of React’s complexity is handling the browser’s legacy” is a real architectural insight — the library’s complexity often mirrors the world’s complexity.

How to do it:

Write a single function updateDom(dom, prevProps, nextProps) that still works now and in Phase 6. In Stage A pass an empty object for prevProps. In Stage B the same function will be used again with the previous props — without changing a line.

This is a forward-compatible design: today’s simple case becomes a special case of tomorrow’s complex case. Finding and handling such places is good library design.
gotchas: removeEventListener requires exactly the same function reference. Therefore keep the old handler in prevProps; otherwise listeners will silently accumulate and a single click will trigger the handler five times.
Calling onClick.toLowerCase().slice(2) gives "click" — correct. But onDoubleClick yields "doubleclick", which is wrong (the real event is "dblclick"). You need to keep a small mapping table.
style can also be provided as a string. Decide and document it in decisions.md — we will only allow objects.

l4_0.name: What JSX actually is
l4_0.desc: Just syntax sugar. The compiler turns it into createElement calls. That's all.
l4_0.what:
JSX is not part of JavaScript. The browser does not understand JSX at all. A compiler (Babel, esbuild, swc) reads it and converts it into normal function calls — before your code runs.

Definition: JSX is a syntax extension that a compiler transforms into plain function calls before the code ever runs.

Analogy: JSX works like a translator that converts your Hindi into English for the boss to hear. The boss (browser) has never heard Hindi. It only knows English.
l4_0.why:
Understanding this is the biggest “aha” moment of the whole project. When you look at JSX in its compiled form, every “magic” of React disappears. <App /> means createElement(App) — and App is just a function.

How to do it:

You need to tell the compiler which function to use. The old way: add a /** @jsx h */ pragma at the top of the file. The new way: set jsxFactory: "h" in the build config.

Remember two rules: lower-case tags become strings (<div> → "div") and upper-case tags become variables (<App> → App). Therefore a component’s name must start with a capital letter — this rule belongs to the compiler, not the library.
gotchas: If a component’s name starts with a lower-case letter, the compiler will turn it into a string and the browser will create an unknown <mycomponent> tag. No error — just nothing will appear.
In JSX you write className instead of class, and htmlFor instead of for — because class and for are reserved words in JavaScript.
JSX must return a single root element. That’s why the Fragment (<>...</>) concept exists. For now we can get by with a wrapper div.

l4_1.name: Without tooling — h(), tagged templates, htm
l4_1.desc: You won’t get JSX syntax but you’ll get all the features. And zero build time.
l4_1.what:
There are three ways without JSX:

1. Write h() directly. Zero setup. It looks a bit bracket-heavy but it’s completely clear what’s happening.
2. Create small helpers — const div = (p, ...c) => h("div", p, ...c). Now you can write div({}, h1({}, "hi")).
3. Tagged template literals — the htm library (3 KB) lets you write html<div></div> in the browser without a build step.
l4_1.why:
It’s important to know that tooling is optional. Many people think React requires webpack/Vite “by default”. It does not. Tooling is a convenience that has its own cost — and you’ll only decide when that cost is justified after you have stood on both sides yourself.

How to do it:

The biggest advantage of zero-tooling: the file you write is the file the browser runs. Debugging in DevTools is trivial, no source maps, no “where did this line come from”. It’s excellent for learning.

The biggest drawback: each import triggers a separate network request, and a 50-file app will feel slow in development. And you won’t get the comfort of JSX.
gotchas: htm parses at runtime, meaning each render incurs a small cost (it caches, but the cost isn’t zero). JSX happens at compile time — zero runtime cost.
Helper tags (div, h1) take up many names in the global namespace. Keep them in an object and destructure.
Without a bundler, the .js extension is mandatory in imports. If you copy code that relies on a bundler, the import will break.

l7_1.name: Keyed reconciliation — create a map and match
l7_1.desc: Create a key→element map of the old children, then apply it to the DOM in the new order.
l7_1.what:
The algorithm is straightforward, three steps:

1. Create a map of the old children: key → oldChild.
2. Loop over the new children. For each, find the old one from the map. If found, UPDATE (and reuse the DOM node); if not found, ADD.
3. Remove any old children that remain (still in the map).

And a fourth thing: fix the order. Reused nodes are at their old positions — they need to be moved to the correct place using insertBefore.
l7_1.why:
This is O(n) — one map and one loop. Without keys, correct matching would be O(n²) (compare each new with each old). A Map data structure reduces the algorithm's complexity by one class — this is a classic practical use of CS.

How to do it:

Cheap way to fix the order: iterate the new children from front to back and place each node with parent.insertBefore(node, nextSibling) at the right spot. If the node is already in the correct place, skip insertBefore (otherwise it's a wasted DOM operation).

React's actual algorithm is a bit smarter (it tracks a "last placed index" to minimize moves), but the idea is exactly the same. We'll write a simple version and note in decisions.md what React adds.
gotchas: Don't call insertBefore on every node indiscriminately. It removes the node and re-inserts it, which can disrupt focus and animations. First check whether the node is already in the correct place.
If you forget to do oldByKey.delete(key), step 3 will delete the node you just reused.
Duplicate keys will leave only one entry in the map and silently discard the rest. Ensure a duplicate key warning is emitted in development mode.

l7_2.name: key is not a prop
l7_2.desc: It is for the reconciler, not for the component. This small design decision is significant.
l7_2.what:
In React, the key never reaches the component. props.key is undefined. It is removed from the props at createElement time and stored separately on the element.

The same applies to ref. Both are "meta props" — for the library, not for the component.
l7_2.why:
Why? Because key is an identity hint, not data. If it were a prop, changing it would count as a "props change" and trigger a re-render — whereas the purpose of a key is to indicate whether this is the same element or a new one. These are two completely different levels.

This is a good general lesson: keep the library's own metadata separate from user data, otherwise they will blend together and become impossible to separate later.

How to do it:

We are currently using props.key (simple), but we should fix this: extract the key from props in createElement and store it as element.key.

This is a small refactor, but do it — because it is your first chance to change your own decision, and writing in decisions.md "Revised D6 because..." is a real engineering journal.
gotchas: After the refactor, leftover props.key may remain in old code. Grep and fix all usages, otherwise keys will silently stop working.
Both numbers and strings are allowed as keys, but in a map 1 and "1" are different keys. Stay consistent — either always convert the key to a string.

l8_0.desc: If element.type is a function, call it and render its result.

Until now, element.type was always a string (e.g., "div"). Now it can also be a function.

This is a big deal: your element tree now contains two kinds of nodes — host nodes (which produce DOM) and composite nodes (which only produce other elements). Every renderer has this two-type distinction, and it becomes even more important in Stage C.

At the top of reconcile, add a check: if (typeof newEl.type === "function").

l8_1.name: useState — the magic of array + index
l8_1.desc: Each component's hooks live in an array, and a pointer advances forward. That's it.
l8_1.what:
The question is: the component function runs again on every render, so where does the state persist?

Answer: outside the component. Each component instance has an associated array — hooks = []. And a pointer hookIndex that increments on each useState call.

The first useState → slot 0. The second → slot 1. The third → slot 2. On the next render the pointer starts again at 0, and in the same order the same slots are used.
l8_1.why:
Now you have the answer to the "rules of hooks". Hooks cannot be placed inside if statements or loops because the entire system relies on call order. If one render runs three hooks and the next runs two, the state from slot 1 will end up in slot 0 — and everything will silently break.

This rule is not an arbitrary React quirk; it is a direct consequence of the design. The design was chosen because the alternative (naming every piece of state) would make the API heavy.

How to do it:

setState is a closure that remembers its index and its fiber. It does three things: write the new value into the slot, and schedule a re-render.

Another essential point: setState(value) should work alongside setState(prev => prev + 1) — because when two updates arrive together, an update based on the previous value gives the correct result.
gotchas: If you check with hooks[i] === undefined, useState(undefined) will never initialize. Use the in operator: !(i in instance.hooks).
An Object.is check is necessary — without it, setState(sameValue) would still trigger a re-render, making infinite loops easy.
If you forget to carry the instance from oldEl, a new hooks array will be created on every render and the state will reset. This is the most common Phase 8 bug.

l8_2.name: setState re-render — and batching
l8_2.desc: Don't render immediately. Do it once in a microtask.
l8_2.what:
The simplest scheduleUpdate does this: run update(App()) immediately. That works, but there's a problem.

If you call setState three times in a click handler, three full re-renders will happen. That's wasteful.
l8_2.why:
Batching means: collect all setState calls in the same "turn" and perform a single re-render. React does this by default (everywhere since React 18). The benefit is straightforward — three times less work. It’s also a very common architectural pattern: don’t do work immediately, put it in a queue and execute it together later.

How to do it:

The simplest batching: keep a flag and use queueMicrotask.

queueMicrotask means "run right after the current synchronous code finishes, but before the browser paints". This is better than setTimeout(fn, 0) because that waits until the next frame.

In Stage C we will improve this — the scheduler will also consider priority.
gotchas: If you read a state variable immediately after setState, you’ll get the old value. It’s "frozen" for the render. This isn’t a bug, it’s by design — the solution is a functional update.
If an error occurs inside queueMicrotask, it can silently disappear. Wrap it in try/catch and console.error.
With batching a new issue appears: if setState runs during a re-render, it can create an infinite loop. Add a depth counter and throw an error after 50 (React does the same).

l9_0.name: Why effect runs after render
l9_0.desc: During render the DOM is incomplete. Effect needs the full DOM.
l9_0.what:
Definition: A side effect is any work that reaches outside the component — network requests, timers, subscriptions, direct DOM measurement, logging.

useEffect(fn, deps) says: "Don't run fn now. Run it after the full render is committed and the DOM is ready."
l9_0.why:
Two reasons:

1. The DOM must be ready. If you need to measure an element’s height or set focus, that element isn’t in the DOM during render.
2. The render should stay pure. If you fetch during render it will run on every render, and in Stage C — where a render can run twice or be cancelled in between — it will cause disaster.

This second reason is deeper. React’s insistence on "keep render pure" exists so that it can pause, discard, and replay a render. That is the whole foundation of Phase 11.

How to do it:

The implementation is straightforward: useEffect itself does not run the effect — it puts it into a queue. After reconciliation finishes, we run the queue.

This "don’t run now, enqueue, run later" pattern appears for the third time in this project (batching, effects, and Stage C’s commit phase). Recognize this pattern — you’ll find it in every large system.
gotchas: Don’t run effects inside reconciliation. The DOM is incomplete at that time and if the effect calls setState you’ll get into recursion.

An effect can call setState inside flushEffects, which will schedule a new render. That’s fine — but clear the queue first (q = effectQueue; effectQueue = []) otherwise the list will keep changing while you’re looping over it.

l9_1.name: Deps array — when to run again
l9_1.desc: Shallow compare. And this is the spot where infinite loops are created.
l9_1.what:
The deps array means: "run the effect again only if one of these values changed."

There are three forms, and all are different:

useEffect(fn) — after every render
useEffect(fn, []) — only once (on mount)
useEffect(fn, [a, b]) — when a or b changes
l9_1.why:
The comparison is shallow — using Object.is on each element. The direct consequence: if a dep is an object, array, or function that is new on every render, it will always appear "changed" and the effect will run each time.

If that effect calls setState, you get a new render, a new object, the effect again, setState… infinite loop. This is the most common React bug and now you know why it happens.

How to do it:

Why not deep compare? Because it would have to walk the entire object tree on every render — expensive and unpredictable. Shallow compare is O(deps.length) and always cheap.

This is a classic trade-off: cheap and predictable, at the cost of requiring the developer to think a bit. React chose this, and useMemo/useCallback are the direct result of that choice — they exist so you can keep references stable.
gotchas: Changing the length of the deps array between renders will break everything — just like hook order. The deps array size must be constant.
Using a function as a dep has the same problem — arrow functions are new on every render. That’s why useCallback exists.
Omitting the deps array (useEffect(fn) without an array) isn’t wrong, but it will run on every render. Do it intentionally, not by accident.

l9_2.name: Cleanup — stop what you started
l9_2.desc: If an effect returns a function, it runs before the next effect and on unmount.
l9_2.what:
If an effect "starts" something — a timer, event listener, subscription, WebSocket — it must also be stopped. Otherwise you get memory leaks or ghost updates (setState on an unmounted component).

The useEffect contract: if you return a function, the library will run it in two places — right before the next effect, and when the component unmounts.
l9_2.why:
The "before the next effect" part is the one most people miss. Imagine: userId changes, the effect runs again. The previous user’s subscription must be stopped first, otherwise two subscriptions will keep running and accumulate.

This is a classic resource lifecycle problem — anything you acquire must be released. Every system has this: file handles, DB connections, locks. React turned it into a simple contract: "what you return is how to clean it up."

How to do it:

Order matters: run the old cleanup first, then the new effect. Reversing that will cause both run together.

You also need to handle the unmount case: when the reconciler REMOVE a component, iterate over all its hooks and run each cleanup — and do the same for its child components (recursively).

Forgetting to run cleanup on unmount is the most hidden bug. Timers keep running and you get "setState on unmounted component" warnings. This gradually slows the whole app.
The cleanup receives the values from the closure at that time, not the latest values. That’s correct — you need to stop the exact resource you opened.

l11_1.name: performUnitOfWork — a node's work
l11_1.desc: Create the DOM (if it doesn't exist), create child fibers, return the next node.
l11_1.what:
A "unit of work" has three tasks:

1. If the fiber doesn't have a DOM node, create it (do not append yet!).
2. Create fibers for its children and link them into the chain.
3. Return the next fiber — the child, or the sibling, or climb up.
l11_1.why:
Each unit is small and bounded — it does the work of a single node, no matter how large the tree is. Therefore the loop can pause after any unit. This provides predictable granularity, which lets the scheduler do its job.

How to do it:

An essential change: Create the DOM but do not append it. Because if we pause midway and some DOM gets appended, the user will see an incomplete UI — which was the R3 issue in Phase 10.

So when will the append happen? After all work is finished, all at once. That is the commit phase of Phase 12. For now we will keep creating and remember one place.

render() no longer renders anything — it only schedules work. The name now feels a bit misleading; React has the same confusion.
You must re-register requestIdleCallback(workLoop) inside the loop, otherwise it will run only once.

l11_2.name: Work loop — pause and resume
l11_2.desc: The entire position is stored in a variable. Pause, give control to the browser, then resume from the same spot.
l11_2.what:
Now see the magic: nextUnitOfWork is a variable that holds our entire position. The loop can pause, the function can return, the browser can do whatever — and when we come back, work will resume from that variable.

This is called resumable computation. It is the whole point of Fibers — everything else (priority, suspense, concurrent) is built on this single property.
l11_2.why:
Once you have resumable work, a lot becomes possible:

• If more important work comes in the middle, do it first (priority)
• Throw the work away if it has gone stale (the user typed more)
• Hold a piece of work back until the data arrives (Suspense)

We won't build any of these — but now you can say how they are possible. And that is exactly what gets asked in interviews.

How to do it:

One small but important detail: we keep a wipRoot (work in progress root) and a currentRoot (what is on the screen right now). Work happens on wipRoot, the screen shows currentRoot.

Having these two separate trees is the foundation of Phase 12. And it's a well-known pattern — in graphics it is called double buffering: write to one buffer, show the other, then swap.
gotchas: If pause is 0, it means your tree is so small that it finishes within a single idle period. Try with 10,000+ nodes and apply CPU throttling.
The deadline for requestIdleCallback depends on the browser's state. Sometimes you get 50 ms, sometimes 1 ms. This is normal — the code should handle both.
Don't place console.log on every unit — it is slow enough to ruin measurements.

Each fiber has an alternate pointer that references the same fiber from the previous render.

There are two trees: the current tree (currently on screen) and the work-in-progress tree (being built). At commit time we simply set currentRoot = wipRoot — and the roles of the two trees swap.

Definition: Double buffering means keeping two versions of a structure — one being displayed, one being written — and swapping them atomically when the new one is complete.
l12_0.why:
Three big benefits:

1. Comparison is free — the old fiber is just a pointer away, no search needed.
2. Cancellation is free — discard the wipRoot and the screen won't notice.
3. Memory reuse — React reuses alternate fibers instead of creating new ones, because allocating thousands of objects each render is expensive.

How to do it:

When we create fibers for a fiber's children, we simultaneously compare them with the previous children (by walking wipFiber.alternate.child). This is the Stage B reconciliation — now it happens on the fiber tree.

The comparison result becomes an effectTag: PLACEMENT (new), UPDATE (props changed), or DELETION (no longer needed).
gotchas: DELETION fibers do not exist in the wip tree (because they are not in the new tree). Therefore they must be stored in a separate deletions array, otherwise the commit will never see them.
Link the alternate both ways (wip.alternate = old, and after commit old.alternate = wip) — otherwise the old tree won't be reachable on the third render.
Clear the deletions array at the start of each new render. If you forget, old deletions will run again.
l12_0.visualCap: Two trees, one swap. Work happens on the WIP tree (can pause or be discarded); the screen shows the current tree. At a single line in commit, their roles switch.

l12_1.name: commitRoot — everything at once
l12_1.desc: A recursive walk, three effectTags, and the DOM changes in a single pass.
l12_1.what:
The commit phase is straightforward: walk the fiber tree and act based on each fiber's effectTag.

PLACEMENT → parentDom.appendChild(fiber.dom)
UPDATE → updateDom(fiber.dom, alternate.props, fiber.props)
DELETION → run cleanup, then parentDom.removeChild
l12_1.why:
And do it using recursion — this is intentional. The commit must not pause. If the commit stops midway, the user will see an incomplete UI, which defeats the design.

This is a key insight: Fiber did not eliminate recursion entirely — it only removed it where pausing was required. The commit is small and fast (because it only contains changes, not the whole tree), so recursion is perfectly fine there.

How to do it:

A small but real detail: finding the parent DOM. Function components have no DOM of their own, so fiber.return.dom can be null. Climb upward until you find a fiber with a DOM.

The same applies to deletion — if the fiber being deleted has no DOM (it is a component), descend into its children until you find a DOM.
gotchas: In the DELETION case you must return — otherwise you will keep traversing the deleted subtree.
If you forget the domParentFiber loop, children of function components will be appended in the wrong place (or cause a crash).
PLACEMENT always uses appendChild, so inserting in the middle can produce the wrong order. For reordering with keys you need insertBefore — this is a known limitation; document it in decisions.md.

l10_0.name: One thread, and its 16 ms budget
l10_0.desc: The browser has 16.7 ms per frame. Your JavaScript consumes some of that.
l10_0.what:
60 fps means 60 frames per second — i.e., one frame is 1000/60 = 16.7ms.

In that 16.7 ms the browser must do everything: run your JavaScript, recalculate styles, layout, paint, composite. If your JavaScript alone takes 100 ms, then 6 frames are lost. The user sees a jerk or freeze.

Definition: A "long task" is any single JavaScript task that occupies the main thread for more than 50 ms. During a long task the page cannot respond to input at all.
l10_0.why:
And the worst part: during that time the click also sits in the queue. The user clicks the button, nothing happens, clicks again. When the JavaScript finishes, both clicks run together. That’s the "app has hung" feeling.

This is not just a performance issue — it’s about user trust. An app that reacts in 100 ms feels "fast"; one that takes 300 ms feels "broken".

How to do it:

Two ways to measure:

1. DevTools > Performance — record, and find the red-triangle "Long Task" blocks. Hover each block to see its duration.
2. PerformanceObserver — capture long tasks directly from code. This also works for production monitoring.
gotchas: The longtask entry only captures tasks longer than 50 ms. 30 ms tasks also consume two frames but won’t appear here.
On a fast laptop the problem stays hidden. Apply 4×–6× CPU throttling in DevTools — then you’ll see what your users see.
Measuring total time isn’t enough. Measure the largest single task — that’s what the user feels.

l10_1.name: Why you can’t pause recursion
l10_1.desc: The call stack is a pile. If you jump out in the middle you’ll lose everything.
l10_1.what:
Imagine you want to pause in the middle of recursion — out of 5,000 nodes you’ve processed 2,000, and now you need to give the browser a frame.

You can’t. Because the whole "where were we" record is stored in the call stack. If you unwind the stack that record is lost. JavaScript has no way to save the stack and resume later.

Analogy: you have opened 10 drawers in a deep cabinet and are now inside the innermost box. You only know "which drawer you came from" because you are standing there right now. If you leave the house you’ll have to come back and find the exact spot again.
l10_1.why:
That’s why Fiber dropped recursion. It’s the biggest architectural insight of the whole project: if you need to pause work, keep the "where are we" record with you, not on the call stack.

How to do it:

Solution: structure the tree so that the next node can be derived from any node — without a stack. In other words each node must know: who its first child is, who its next sibling is, and who its parent is.

These three pointers — child, sibling, return — together turn a tree into a traversable list. That is the Fiber.

Now "where you are" is just a variable: nextUnitOfWork. Keep it, pause, and later resume from the same spot. That’s it.
gotchas: Generators (function*) can also pause, and React tried this early on. It was dropped because a generator can only resume from its own position — you can’t change priority or throw work away midway. Knowing this looks good in an interview.
Web Workers could offload the main thread — but they can’t touch the DOM. So that path is closed.

l10_2.name: Shape of the solution — units of work
l10_2.desc: Break the work into small chunks, after each chunk ask "any time left?"
l10_2.what:
The new model will be:

1. The whole work breaks into small "units" — one unit = the work of one node.
2. A loop runs that processes one unit, then asks "does the browser need to do something?"
3. If yes, the loop stops. The browser paints, listens for clicks.
4. As soon as the browser is free, the loop resumes from where it left off.

This is called cooperative scheduling — the work voluntarily yields control periodically.
l10_2.why:
Total time will increase — yielding has its own cost. But the app will feel alive. This is a deep trade-off: throughput vs responsiveness.

This also underpins React’s entire "concurrent" story. It’s a design philosophy: a 100 ms freeze feels bad to the user, while a smooth 120 ms operation feels good — even if it actually takes a bit longer.

How to do it:

There are two APIs that answer "does the browser need to do something?":

requestIdleCallback(cb) — the browser calls you when it’s idle, and deadline.timeRemaining() tells you how much time is left. Perfect fit — but not supported in Safari and timing isn’t predictable.

MessageChannel — a way to schedule a "next immediate task", faster than setTimeout(0) (which has a minimum 4 ms clamp). React uses this and keeps its own 5 ms budget.

We will start with requestIdleCallback (easier to understand), and as a stretch goal build a MessageChannel-based scheduler.
gotchas: requestIdleCallback is not available in Safari. You’ll need a small polyfill (based on setTimeout) or implement a MessageChannel scheduler.
Calling timeRemaining() after every unit is also a bit expensive. React checks not after every unit but after several units.
If a single unit itself takes 16 ms (a very heavy component), yielding provides no benefit. Therefore units must stay small — one node per unit.

l11_0.desc: Extra information needed to work with an element. And a new relationship.
l11_0.what:
A fiber node contains:

type, props — from the element
dom — the actual DOM node for this fiber (if it’s a host fiber)
child — the first child (not all, just the first)
sibling — the next sibling
return — the parent (called "return" because when work is done we “return” here)
alternate — the same fiber from the previous render (Phase 12)
effectTag — what to do: PLACEMENT / UPDATE / DELETION

Instead of storing all children of a node in an array, keep only the first child and link the rest as a sibling chain — that’s the trick. This lets you find the next node from any node using a fixed rule, without an array index or a stack.

Definition: A fiber is a plain object representing one unit of work, holding both the element’s data and the links needed to traverse the tree without recursion.

Remember: the fiber tree is the same element tree, just connected differently. The data is the same — only the shape of the relationships changes. Once you get this, the fear of Fiber disappears.

l14_0.name: Event delegation and synthetic events
l14_0.desc: Listener on each node vs a single listener on the root. And what React chose and why.
l14_0.what:
Until now we attach a direct addEventListener to every DOM node. It works, but there are three problems:

1. 1000 buttons = 1000 listeners = memory usage.
2. On every update remove the old one and add a new one — works.
3. In older browsers event behavior was different.

Event delegation means: attach a single listener on the root. The event will bubble up there, and event.target will reveal which element was actually the source.
l14_0.why:
Before React 17, React attached all listeners to the document; now it attaches them to the root container. This changed because a page can host two React apps, and document-level delegation would cause them to clash.

This is a good lesson: architectural decisions change when the context changes. What was correct in React 16 became incorrect in React 17 — because the world changed, not the code.

How to do it:

Synthetic event is a wrapper object built on top of the browser's native event so that behavior is the same across browsers.

We will build a simple version: listeners on the root, a map domNode → handlers, and we will simulate bubbling ourselves (climb from the target up and run each parent’s handler).

And write honestly in decisions.md: this trade-off was not required for our project — we built it to learn. The real trade-off appears when there are thousands of nodes.
gotchas: Some events do not bubble — focus, blur, mouseenter, mouseleave. React uses focusin/focusout for them or listens in the capture phase.
Use WeakMap, not Map — otherwise deleted DOM nodes will remain in memory (memory leak).
stopPropagation now works on two levels: your synthetic bubbling and the native DOM. Handle both or the behavior will be surprising.

l14_1.name: Context — passing data down
l14_1.desc: Store the provider value on the fiber, and let the consumer climb the return chain upward to find it.
l14_1.what:
Problem: to pass a theme or user five levels down you have to pass a prop at every level — prop drilling.

Context’s answer: a Provider stores a value in the tree, and any component below it can take that value directly.
l14_1.why:
The implementation has a beauty: we already have a return pointer that links each fiber to its parent. So the consumer only needs to climb upward until it finds a matching provider.

This is a good example of how a solid data structure makes later features easy. We built fibers for scheduling — and context came for free.

How to do it:

createContext(defaultValue) returns an object that contains a Provider component.

In useContext(ctx): start from wipFiber and climb the return chain upward; when a fiber’s type === ctx.Provider, return its props.value. If none is found, return the default.

And write an honest note: our context will re-render the entire tree when the value changes, because our setState re-renders the whole root. React also actually re-renders only the consumers, but it needs a subscription mechanism for that. This "known limitation" should be documented.
gotchas: If the provider’s value is an object, a new one will be created on every render, causing consumers to re-render each time. Keep it stable with useMemo — the same dependency-array issue.
Don’t use context as a "global state". It is for dependency injection (theme, locale, auth), not for high-frequency data.
Our implementation climbs the return chain on every render — O(depth). React maintains a stack that is O(1). Document this limitation.

l14_2.name: Architecture review — what will scale
l14_2.desc: Look back. Count the layers, write the limits, and suggest the next step.
l14_2.what:
Now you have built a library. The final task is to understand it — to view your own work from the outside.

Answer four questions:

1. Which layer knows what, and what it doesn’t know?
2. Which part will work with a different renderer, and which won’t?
3. Where are there O(n) operations and where is there a risk of O(n²)?
4. What will the next three features be and which layer will they belong to?
l14_2.why:
This is not just documentation. It is the work that distinguishes a senior engineer from a junior engineer. A junior explains what they built. A senior explains what they chose, what they left out, and when a decision might become wrong.

Practically, this document will be the most read part of your project.

How to do it:

Run a scalability checklist. For each item include a measured number or an honest "don’t know":

• Mount and update time on 100 / 1,000 / 10,000 nodes
• Deeply nested tree (500 levels) — does it crash?
• Reversing a 10,000-item list — how many DOM moves?
• Memory: how much RAM do 10,000 fibers use?
• Bundle size (minified + gzip)
• How many public API functions are there? (fewer = better)
gotchas: The commit phase is still recursive — on a tree deeper than 500 levels it can cause a stack overflow. This is a real known limitation; document it and, if possible, make it iterative.
Don’t claim "it scales" until you have measured it. Include a number with each claim or write "don’t know".
performance.memory exists only in Chrome and is approximate. Don’t rely on it heavily.

l12_2.name: Why the render phase should be pure
l12_2.desc: This phase can pause, be cancelled, or run twice. Therefore the rules are strict.
l12_2.what:
Now you can see why React is so insistent:

• "Don’t perform side effects during render"
• "Don’t mutate props or state"
• "Components render twice in StrictMode"

Because in the render phase your component function can run multiple times, and its work can be discarded. If it performed a fetch or changed a global, it would run twice or be incomplete.
l12_2.why:
This is the deepest lesson of the entire library: a performance feature (interruptibility) imposed a constraint (purity) on the API.

And this is a general truth — architectural decisions always surface at the top level. You choose something in one layer, and its cost appears in the user-facing API. It cannot be hidden, only well explained.

How to do it:

Create a small StrictMode in your library: in dev mode call each component function twice and compare the results. Issue a warning if they differ.

It’s about 10 lines and it becomes the most "senior" feature of your project — because it shows that you understand not just the feature, but its cost as well.
gotchas: Rendering twice will halve performance in development. That’s fine — keep the flag off in production.
If you compare with JSON.stringify, functions (event handlers) won’t match. You’ll need to sanitize (remove) them.
StrictMode also runs effects twice (React 18) — to catch cleanup mistakes. This is a stretch goal.

A new task also appears: the function component’s fiber will now be handled by updateFunctionComponent, which sets the hooks context before calling the component.

And setState will no longer update directly. It will create a new wipRoot and set nextUnitOfWork. The work loop will pick it up automatically. This is one level above Stage B — state updates and rendering are now completely separate.

Create a new array for wipFiber.hooks on each render; don’t reuse the old one — otherwise old and new hooks will mix.
When creating wipRoot inside setState, use currentRoot.props, not a component’s — we are re-rendering the entire tree.

l13_1.name: useRef, useMemo, useCallback — all the same thing
l13_1.desc: A slot that persists across renders. Just different forms of the same thing.
l13_1.what:
Now see how small the other hooks are:

useRef = a slot containing an object {current: x} that never changes.
useMemo = a slot with a value and deps. If deps are the same, return the previous value; otherwise recalculate.
useCallback = useMemo(() => fn, deps). That’s it.
useReducer = useState where you provide the way to turn an action into new state.
l13_1.why:
When you implement these four hooks yourself, the entire hooks API will start to feel like a small consistent primitive. And that’s a core library-design lesson: build one primitive, and put everything else on top of it.

React itself has only two primitives — useState (which is essentially useReducer) and useEffect. Everything else is a combination of these two.

How to do it:

Keep the shape of every hook the same: { ...data, deps }. Write a small helper getHook() that extracts the previous hook and creates a new slot. This reduces each hook to 5–6 lines.
gotchas: In useRef, return the existing hook object; don’t create a new one — otherwise ref.current resets on every render and defeats the purpose.
The function passed to useMemo runs during render, so don’t put side effects in it. That’s the purity rule.
useCallback doesn’t call the function; it only remembers it. In useMemo(() => fn), the arrow function returns fn without calling it.
l13_1.visualCap: The entire hooks API stands on two primitives. After seeing this pyramid, any new hook will show you “how it should be built” on its own.

l13_2.name: Effects on the fiber — and after commit
l13_2.desc: Effect list lives on the fiber, and flushes together after the commit phase.
l13_2.what:
The effect logic is the same as Stage B, only two things change:

1. The effect hook lives on the fiber and comes from the previous alternate.
2. Effects run after the commit phase, because that’s when the DOM is ready.

And a new detail: when to run cleanup. The previous cleanup should run during commit (before the DOM is removed), and the new effect runs after commit.
l13_2.why:
Now you can implement the difference between useEffect and useLayoutEffect yourself:

useLayoutEffect — runs immediately after commit, synchronously, before the browser paints. This lets you measure the DOM and modify it in the same frame without flicker.
useEffect — runs after commit, but asynchronously (after paint). This does not block painting.

This is a two-line code difference, but a huge difference for the user. And now you will demonstrate that difference by building it, not by memorizing.

How to do it:

At the end of commit, run two queues: first layout effects (sync), then passive effects via queueMicrotask or requestIdleCallback.

Run cleanup during commit, and the effect after commit. Doing it the other way round will let the old resource linger with the new one for a while.
Don’t forget to handle the ref prop — in createDom set ref.current = dom as soon as the DOM node is created, otherwise useRef won’t work for DOM elements.

l4_2.name: With tooling — what you get, what you lose
l4_2.desc: Add Vite/esbuild and honestly write the accounting on both sides.
l4_2.what: A bundler (Vite, esbuild, webpack) does three things: transform (JSX → JS), bundle (50 file → 1 file), and dev server (HMR, fast reload).
l4_2.why:
What you get: the comfort of JSX; a single network request; a smaller bundle through minify + tree-shaking; HMR, which reloads code while keeping state; imports from node_modules (without writing a URL); TypeScript, CSS modules, images — everything.

What you give up: your code and the browser's code are now different — you need source maps for debugging; one more config file that will break; 200MB in node_modules; build time; and the biggest thing — one more thing you'll have to understand.

How to do it:

This decision isn't mechanical, it's situational. A small learning project, one or two files, for learning → zero tooling is better, because you see exactly what is running. A big app, a team, TypeScript, 50+ files → the cost of tooling is paid back.

This question comes up in interviews. The right answer isn't "use Vite" — the right answer is "what is this giving me in exchange for what, and which matters more in my case".
gotchas: If you forget to set jsxFactory, esbuild will give "React is not defined" — because the default factory is React.createElement.
Don’t treat HMR as a "reload". Reload discards state, while HMR only replaces the changed module and preserves state. This is the real productivity difference.
Measure bundle size from a production build, not from dev. The dev bundle is intentionally larger and unminified.
l4_2.visualCap: Two paths, one destination. Tooling doesn’t unlock a feature — it only provides convenience and, in return, adds a layer of indirection.

l5_0.name: Identity — why a DOM node must stay alive
l5_0.desc: Focus, scroll, selection, animation, video playback — all live inside the node, not in your state.
l5_0.what:
A DOM node is not just "what is displayed". Inside it there is a lot of hidden state that isn’t present anywhere in your JS:

  • Which element has focus
  • Where the text selection starts and ends
  • The scroll position
  • Which frame a CSS transition/animation is on
  • Which second a
  • What the user typed in an uncontrolled input

All of this disappears as soon as the node is deleted. Creating a new node does not bring it back.
l5_0.why:
This is called identity: "is this the same node or a new one". It is the real purpose of the entire reconciliation. People think the reconciler exists for speed — it does not. Speed is a bonus. The real reason is correctness: a DOM node must stay alive or the app breaks.

This is a great interview point because most people recite the "virtual DOM is fast" mantra.

How to do it:

The solution is simple: remember the old tree, compare it with the new one, and do not touch any node that is the same — just update its changed props.

Therefore the first step of Stage B is not code, it is data: we need a place to store the relationship between the old tree and its DOM nodes.
gotchas: Don’t try to fix focus by "refocusing after render". It will break cursor position, selection, and IME (Hindi/Chinese typing).
This problem isn’t limited to inputs. Third-party libraries (chart, map, editor) that hold onto a DOM node break completely.

l5_1.name: Performance — how much work is wasted
l5_1.desc: Rebuilding 5,000 nodes for a single character change. Measure, don’t guess.
l5_1.what:
In Stage A each update does work proportional to the size of the tree, no matter how small the change. A counter going from 0 to 1 rebuilds the entire tree.

Creating DOM is far more expensive than creating JS objects, because every createElement forces the browser to build internal structures, and after appendChild it must perform layout and paint again.
l5_1.why:
Without numbers it’s just a feeling. With numbers it becomes engineering. And the habit — "measure first, then optimize" — is the biggest lesson from this whole project.

How to do it:

Measure milliseconds with performance.now(), and record in Chrome DevTools’ Performance tab. Look for two things: Scripting (JS) and Rendering + Painting (browser work).

An essential observation: if your update takes more than 16 ms, you cannot achieve 60 fps — the browser has only 16.7 ms per frame. Remember this number; it will become the whole story in Phase 10.
gotchas: Don’t draw a conclusion from a single measurement. The first run is always slow (JIT hasn’t warmed up). Run a warm-up pass separately.
console.log itself is slow. Don’t log inside the loop; only log at the end.
Keeping DevTools open changes timings. Close it and measure again.
l5_1.visualCap: A tiny change, but work equal to the whole tree. The green nodes were exactly the same — breaking and rebuilding them was 100% wasted effort.

l5_2.name: Shape of the solution — diffing
l5_2.desc: Remember the old, compare with the new, find the differences. And do it in O(n).
l5_2.what:
The problem statement is now clear: given an old tree and a new tree, tell what needs to change in the DOM.

This is a well-known computer-science problem — tree diffing. And the bad news is that the best general tree-diff algorithm is O(n³). 1,000 nodes = 1,000,000,000 operations. Wasteful.
l5_2.why:
React made this O(n), but not for free — it assumes two assumptions. This is the biggest architectural lesson of the whole project: when the exact solution is expensive, shrink the problem — thoughtfully, in code.

How to do it:

React’s two assumptions:

1. Different type = different tree. If the old element was <div> and the new one is <p>, don’t compare — discard the whole subtree and create a new one. This holds true in about 99% of cases.
2. Identity comes from the key. In a list, identify children by key instead of position. (Phase 7)

This is a heuristic — not always optimal, but practically sufficient. Stating that "this is a heuristic, not an algorithm" will set you apart from everyone else.
gotchas: These assumptions are not "React’s shortcomings" — they are deliberate trade-offs. If you change a <div> to a <span>, the entire subtree is rebuilt, and you should know that.
The purpose of diffing is correctness (identity) before speed. This point is often forgotten.

l6_1.name: reconcile() — four cases
l6_1.desc: ADD, REMOVE, REPLACE, UPDATE. The whole function comes from this table.
l6_1.what:
Function signature: reconcile(parentDom, oldEl, newEl, index). index is needed because we must know which child this is inside the parent (parentDom.childNodes[index]).

Four cases, check them in this order:

1. !oldEl → ADD: create a new DOM, parentDom.appendChild
2. !newEl → REMOVE: parentDom.removeChild(parentDom.childNodes[index])
3. oldEl.type !== newEl.type → REPLACE: create a new one, replaceChild
4. same type → UPDATE: pass the DOM, update props, recurse children
l6_1.why:
These four cases are exhaustive — there is no fifth case. This is a hallmark of good library design: shrink the state space so you can write all cases and prove that none are missed.

How to do it:

In the UPDATE case there are three steps, in this order:

1. newEl.dom = oldEl.dom — pass the DOM node forward.
2. updateDom(dom, oldEl.props, newEl.props) — the Phase 3 function, unchanged.
3. Loop over children: go up to Math.max(oldChildren.length, newChildren.length), and for each index call reconcile(dom, oldChildren[i], newChildren[i], i).

Math.max is used because the number of children can change — undefined on either side will automatically become an ADD or REMOVE case. This is a small elegance.
gotchas: When removing, iterate backwards (i = n-1 down to 0), otherwise removing a node shifts later indexes and the wrong node gets deleted.
parentDom.childNodes[index] remains valid only as long as you haven't added or removed any nodes inside the loop. Therefore performing REMOVE separately, after the loop, is safer.
Forgetting to set newEl.dom — in the next render oldEl.dom will be undefined and everything will silently break.
l6_1.visualCap: The full decision tree of reconcile. These four paths are the entire logic of Stage B — there is no fifth case.

l6_2.name: The cost of recursion — and a warning
l6_2.desc: It works, it's fast, but once it starts it cannot stop.
l6_2.what:
Your reconciler is now fast and correct. But it has a property that you won't see yet: it is not interruptible.

As soon as update() is called, it will recurse over the entire tree. It will not stop in the middle. JS is single-threaded, meaning that while this function is running, the browser cannot do anything — it cannot listen to clicks, cannot paint, cannot scroll.
l6_2.why:
In small apps this is perfectly fine — 100 nodes finish in 1 ms. But with 10,000 nodes it becomes a 200 ms “long task” and the user will see the app freeze. This is the wall of Phase 10, and Fiber was born from this exact problem.

How to do it:

Do nothing for now. Just write in notes/: "reconcile uses recursion, so once it starts it cannot stop. To stop it you must unwind the call stack."

Make this a habit — whenever you notice a design limitation, write it down immediately, even if you’re not solving it yet. This “known limitations” list is the most valuable document in production systems.

l7_0.name: When matching by position breaks
l7_0.desc: Insert an item in the middle of a list — everything shifts by one position.
l7_0.what:
Imagine the list is [B, C] and the new list is [A, B, C]. If you compare by position:

index 0: old B vs new A → change the text
index 1: old C vs new B → change the text
index 2: nothing vs new C → create a new one

Result: all three rows were touched, even though only one row was actually added. And if the rows contained inputs, their focus and typed text moved to the wrong row.
l7_0.why:
This is not just a performance issue — it is a correctness issue. In a todo list a checkbox will be ticked on the wrong item. In a chat the input text will stick to the wrong message. That’s why React’s “Each child should have a unique key” warning is a serious warning, not a nuisance.

How to do it:

The fix is to change the basis of matching. Instead of position, use a stable identifier — key. Now the reconciler says: “Which element in the old list had key = B? Match it with the new element that also has key = B, even if it is now at position 1.”
gotchas: Using the index as a key is equivalent to not providing keys — the index is still a position. It is only safe when the list never reorders, inserts, or deletes.
Do not use Math.random() or Date.now() as a key. A new key on every render means everything is new on every render — worse than Stage A.
Keys do not need to be globally unique — they only need to be unique among their siblings.
